project.title: Annotating Religion: An Audiovisual Corpus of Ritual, Sound, and Spirituality in Golden Age Mexican Cinema
project.description: The project, created by Ivan Brea, explores the representation and mediation of religion, spirituality, and Catholic traditions in Mexican cinema during the Golden Age of Mexican Cinema (approximately 1935-1955). Titled “Annotating Religion: An Audiovisual Corpus of Ritual, Sound, and Spirituality in Golden Age Mexican Cinema”, the project examines how cinema negotiated the place of religion within an increasingly modernizing and secular Mexican nation. Through a curated selection of three films directed by Emilio “El Indio” Fernández, one of the most influential filmmakers of Mexico’s Golden Age of Cinema, “María Candelaria” (1943), “Enamorada” (1946), and “Río Escondido” (1947), the project investigates how religious experience is constructed and made perceptible through cinematic form. It examines how Fernández’s films weave Catholic imagery, religious rituals, sacred spaces, and spiritual symbolism into broader representations of Mexicanidad, national identity, and postrevolutionary modernity, paying particular attention to ritual, prayer, religious speech, bodily gestures, sacred objects, and audiovisual elements such as hymns, bells, religious music, and silence. What makes the project particularly compelling is its emphasis on sound and sensory experience as dimensions of cinematic religiosity that often receive less scholarly attention. Using AVAnnotate, the project brings together timestamped annotations, conceptual tags, and comparative analysis in a searchable audiovisual corpus, allowing viewers to trace recurring religious motifs and formal techniques across films. By bringing together Film Studies, Cultural Studies, Religious Studies, and Digital Humanities, the project offers a new approach to understanding how Mexican cinema represented Catholicism and negotiated questions of modernity, Mexicanidad, spectatorship, and national identity.
